#Text=The hollow channel left by the share of the plough is called
#Text= the furrow, the raised land between two furrows is called the ridge
#Text= (_porca_,) because there the seed is as it were laid upon an altar
#Text= (_porricere_) to secure a crop, for when the entrails are offered to
#Text= the gods this word _porricere_ is used to describe the oblation.

#Text= 2° _March 24-May 7_
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXX.
#Text=These are the things to be done during the second season between
#Text= the vernal equinox and the rising of the Pleiades.
#Text=Weed the corn land,
#Text= break up old sod, cut the willows, close the pastures (to the stock)
#Text= and complete any thing left undone in the preceding season.
#Text=Plant
#Text= trees before the buds shoot and they begin to blossom, for deciduous
#Text= trees are not fit to transplant after they put forth leaves.
#Text=Plant and
#Text= prune your olives.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 3° _May 7-June 24_
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXXI.
#Text=These are the things to be done during the third season between
#Text= the rising of the Pleiades and the summer solstice.
#Text=Dig the young
#Text= vines or plough them, and afterwards put the land in good order; that
#Text= is to say, fine the soil so that no clods shall remain.
#Text=This is called
#Text= fining the soil (_occare_) because it breaks down (_occidare_) the
#Text= clods.
#Text=Thin out the vines, but let it be done by one who knows
#Text= how, for this operation which is considered of great importance is
#Text= performed only on vines and not on the orchard.
#Text=To thin a vine is to
#Text= select and reserve the one, two and some times even three best new
#Text= tendrils sprung from the stem of the vine, cutting off all the others,
#Text= lest the stem may be unable to furnish nourishment for those which
#Text= have been reserved.
#Text=So in a nursery it is the custom to cut it back
#Text= at first so that the vine may grow with a stronger stem and may have
#Text=greater strength to produce fruitful tendrils: for a stem which grows
#Text= slender like a rush is sterile through weakness and cannot throw out
#Text= tendrils.
#Text=Thus it is the custom to call a weak stem a flag, and
#Text= a strong stem, which bears grapes, a palm.
#Text=The name _flagellum_,
#Text= indicating something as unstable as a breeze, is derived from
#Text= _flatus_, by the change of a letter, just as in the case of the word
#Text= _flabellum_, which means fly fan.
#Text=The name _palma_, which is given
#Text= to those vine shoots which are fruitful in grapes, was it seems, at
#Text= first, parilema, derived from _parire_ (to produce), whence by a
#Text= change of letters, such as we find in many instances, it came to be
#Text= called _palma_.
#Text=From another part of the vine springs the _capreolus_, which is a
#Text= little spiral tendril, like a curled hair, by means of which the vine
#Text= holds on while it creeps towards the place of which it would take
#Text= possession, from which quality of taking hold of things (_capere_) it
#Text= is called _capreolus_.
#Text=All forage crops should be saved at this season; first, basil, then
#Text= mixed fodder (_farrago_)[87] and vetch, and last of all the hay.
#Text=Our
#Text=name for basil is _ocinum_, which is derived from the Greek word
#Text= [Greek: ocheos] and signifies that it comes quickly, like the pot herb
#Text= of the same name.
#Text=It has this name also because it quickens the action
#Text= of the bowels of cattle and so is fed to them as a purgative.
#Text=It is
#Text= cut green from a bean field before the pods are formed.
#Text=On the other
#Text= hand that forage which is cut with a sickle from a field in which
#Text= barley and vetch and other legumes have been sown in mixture for
#Text= forage, is called _farrago_ from the instrument (_ferro_) with which
#Text= it is cut, or perhaps because it was first sown in the stubble of a
#Text= field of corn (_far_).
#Text=It is fed to horses and other cattle in the
#Text= spring to purge and to fatten them.
#Text=Vetch (_vicia_) is so called from its quality of conquering
#Text= (_vincire_) because this plant, like the vine, has tendrils by means
#Text= of which it creeps twisting upward on the stalks of lupines or other
#Text= plants where it clings until it over-tops its host.
#Text=If you have irrigated meadows, proceed to water them at this season,
#Text= as soon as you have saved the hay.
#Text=During droughts water your grafted fruit trees every evening.
#Text=They
#Text= probably derive their name, (_poma_), from their appetite for drink
#Text= (_potus_).
#Text=
#Text=

#Text= 4° _June 24-July 21_
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXXII.
#Text=During the fourth season between the summer solstice and the
#Text= rising of the Dog Star most farmers make their harvest, because it is
#Text= claimed that to mature properly corn should be allowed fifteen days to
#Text= germinate and shoot, fifteen days to bloom and fifteen days to ripen.
#Text=Finish your ploughing: it will be more profitable in proportion as the
#Text= earth is ploughed warm, when the land is broken up, fine it, that is,
#Text= work it again in order that all the clods may be reduced, for at the
#Text= first ploughing large clods are always turned up.
#Text=This is the time
#Text= also to sow vetch, lentils, the small variety of chick peas, pulse
#Text=(_ervilia_) and the other things which we call legumes, but which
#Text= others, as for example the Gauls, call _legarica_, both of which names
#Text= come from the practice of picking their fruit (_legere_) because they
#Text= are not cut but gathered.
#Text=Work the old vines a second time and the young ones thrice, especially
#Text= if there are any clods left.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 5° _July 21-September 26_
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXXIII.
#Text=During the fifth season between the rising of the Dog Star
#Text= and the autumn equinox thresh your straw and rick it, continue the
#Text= harrowing of your fallow land, prune your fruit trees, and mow your
#Text= irrigated meadow the second time.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 6° _September 26-October 28_
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXXIV.
#Text=The authorities advise you to begin to sow at the commencement
#Text= of the sixth season immediately after the autumn equinox and to keep
#Text= it up for the following 91 days, but not to attempt to sow any thing
#Text= after the winter solstice, unless it is absolutely necessary, because
#Text= seed sown before the winter solstice germinates in seven days, while
#Text= that sown later hardly ever sprouts for 40 days.
#Text=In like manner the authorities say that you should not begin your
#Text= sowing before the equinox, lest continued rains cause the seed to rot
#Text= in the ground.
#Text=The best time to plant beans is at the setting of the
#Text= Pleiades, but gather the grapes and make the vintage between the
#Text= equinox and the setting of the Pleiades.
#Text=Immediately afterward begin
#Text= to prune the vines, to propagate them and plant fruit trees, but in
#Text= those regions where the frost comes early it is better to postpone
#Text= these operations until the following spring.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 7° _October 28-December 24._
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXXV.
#Text=These are the things to do during the seventh season between
#Text= the setting of the Pleiades and the winter solstice.
#Text=Plant lilies and
#Text= crocuses and propagate roses, which may be done by making cuttings
#Text= about three inches in length from a stem already rooted, set these out
#Text= and later, after they have formed their own roots, transplant them.
#Text=The cultivation of violets has no place on a farm because they require
#Text= elevated beds for which the soil is scraped up and these are damaged
#Text= or even washed away by heavy rains, thus wasting the fertility of the
#Text= land.
#Text=At any time of the year between the rising of the west wind and
#Text= the rising of Arcturus (February-September) it is proper to transplant
#Text= from the seed beds thyme, an herb, which owes its name, _serpyllum_,
#Text= to its creeping habit (_quod serpit_).
#Text=This is the season also to
#Text= dig new ditches, clean the old ones, and to prune the trees in the
#Text=arbustum and the vines which are married to them, but be careful that
#Text= you suspend most of your work during the fifteen days before and after
#Text= the winter solstice: it is fitting, however, to set out some trees
#Text= during this period, as, for example, elms.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 8° _December 24-February 7_
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= XXXVI.
#Text=These are the things to do during the eighth season between the
#Text= winter solstice and the rising of the west wind.
#Text=Drain the fields, if
#Text= any water is standing on them, but if they are dry and the land is
#Text= friable, harrow them.
#Text=Prune the vines and the orchard.
#Text=When it is not
#Text= fitting to work in the fields then those things should be done which
#Text= can be done under cover during the winter twilight.
#Text=All these rules should be written out and posted in the farmstead and
#Text= the overseer especially should have them at the tip of his tongue.
#Text=_Of the four methods of propagating plants_
#Text=
#Text= XXXIX.
#Text=The second operation, namely that of propagating, must be
#Text= considered in relation to the proper time for sowing each kind of
#Text= seed, for this concerns the aspect of the field you are to sow and the
#Text= season fitting for what you are to plant.
#Text=Do we not see some things
#Text= grow best in the spring, others in summer, some in autumn, and others
#Text= again in winter?
#Text=For each plant is sowed or propagated or harvested in
#Text= season according to its nature: so while most trees are grafted most
#Text= successfully in spring, rather than the autumn, yet figs may be
#Text= grafted at the summer solstice, and cherries even in winter.
#Text=And since there are four methods of propagation of plants, by nature
#Text= and by the several processes of art, namely: transplanting from one
#Text= place to another, as is done in layering vines, what is called cuttage
#Text= or propagating quick sets cut from trees, and graftage, which consists
#Text= in transferring scions from one tree to another, let us consider at
#Text= what season and in what locality you should do each of these things.
#Text=_Of racking wine_
#Text=
#Text= LXV.
#Text=When the must is stored in the vat to make wine, it should not be
#Text= racked off while it is fermenting nor until this process has advanced
#Text= so far that the wine may be considered to be made.
#Text=If you wish to
#Text= drink old wine, it is not made until a year is completed; when it is a
#Text= year old, then draw it out.
#Text=But if your vineyard contains that kind
#Text= of grape which turns sour early, you should eat the fruit, or sell it
#Text= before the succeeding vintage.
#Text=There are kinds of wine, like that of
#Text= Falernum, which improve the longer you keep them.
#Text=_Of preserved olives_
#Text=
#Text= LXVI.
#Text=If you attempt to eat white olives immediately after you have
#Text= put them up and before they are cured your palate will reject them on
#Text= account of their bitterness (and the same is true of the black olive)
#Text= unless you dip them in salt to make them palatable.
#Text=_Of nuts, dates and figs_
#Text=
#Text= LXVII.
#Text=The sooner you use nuts, dates and figs after they have been
#Text= stored, the more palatable they will be, for by keeping figs lose
#Text= their flavour, dates rot and nuts dry up.
#Text=_Of stored fruits_
#Text=
#Text= LXVIII.
#Text=Fruits which are strung, such as grapes, apples and sorbs show
#Text= by their appearance when they may be taken down for use, for by their
#Text= change of colour and shrinking they reveal themselves as destined to
#Text= the garbage pile unless they are eaten in time.
#Text=Sorbs which have been
#Text= laid by when they are already dead-ripe should be used promptly, but
#Text= those which were picked green are slower to decay: for green fruit in
#Text= the store house must there go through the process of ripening which
#Text= was denied it on the tree.

#Text=And such is
#Text= the fact no doubt, that soil is the best which has the savour of a
#Text= perfume.
#Text=If the question should be put to us, what is this odour of
#Text= the earth that is held in such estimation; our answer is that it
#Text=is the same that is often to be recognized at the moment of sunset
#Text= without the necessity even of turning up the ground, at the spots
#Text= where the extremities of the rainbow have been observed to meet the
#Text= earth: as also, when after long continued drought, the rain has soaked
#Text= the ground.
#Text=Then it is that the earth exhales the divine odour that is
#Text= so peculiarly its own, and to which, imparted to it by the sun, there
#Text= is no perfume however sweet that can possibly be compared.
#Text=It is this
#Text= odour which the earth, when turned up, ought to emit, and which, when
#Text= once found, can never deceive any person: and this will be found the
#Text= best criterion for judging of the quality of the soil.
#Text=Such, too, is
#Text= the odour that is usually perceived in land newly cleared when an
#Text= ancient forest has been just cut down; its excellence is a thing that
#Text= is universally admitted.]
